## Claims by unit

### I. Greeting (1–2)

**C1.** Green: Jude’s opening follows ancient epistolary architecture but “modifies the extant literary conventions by giving them a distinct Christian orientation.”  
- Quote: “The author constructs the opening of this letter in accordance with the architecture of ancient epistles yet modifies the extant literary conventions by giving them a distinct Christian orientation.”  
- Locus: L1318  
- Targets: `jude`, `gene-green`, `green-jude-2peter-becnt`

**C2.** Green: Author self-names as “slave of Jesus Christ and brother of James”; readers are “the called”; greeting is Christianized.  
- Quote: “The author names himself yet demonstrates his authority as the ‘slave of Jesus Christ and brother of James’ (v. 1). The readers/hearers of the letter are known by their status as the called people of God.”  
- Locus: L1318  
- Targets: `jude`, `jude-brother-of-jesus`, `james-the-just`

**C3.** Green: “Kept for Christ Jesus” and “called” function as counterpoints to heretical incursion before the theme in v. 3.  
- Quote: “They have been summoned by God and ‘kept for Christ Jesus,’ affirmations that serve as counterpoints to the heretics’ incursion and persuasion.”  
- Locus: L1318  
- Targets: `jude`, `gene-green`

**C4.** Green: Jude’s purpose is to warn against heretics who “distorted the doctrine of grace and turned it into an excuse for moral license.”  
- Quote: “Jude’s objective in composing this letter was to warn the church against the incursion of heretics who had distorted the doctrine of grace and turned it into an excuse for moral license.”  
- Locus: L1339  
- Targets: `jude`, `gene-green`

**C5.** Green: The letter is a “surrogate for his presence” as correction of error; ancient letters shortened distance (citing Seneca, Ep. mor. 40.1; amanuensis/subscript practice).  
- Quote: “Jude’s letter is a surrogate for his presence as he seeks to correct the error that had invaded the church. The letter and the person could not be separated.”  
- Locus: L1339  
- Targets: `jude`, `gene-green`

**C6.** Green: “Jude” (Ἰούδας) is “extremely common”; this Jude is “brother of James” and “half brother of Jesus” (Matt. 13:55; Mark 6:3; intro authorship).  
- Quote: “This Jude, however, is the ‘brother of James’ and the half brother of Jesus (see Matt. 13:55; Mark 6:3; and ‘Authorship of Jude’ in the introduction).”

### II.A Purpose (3–4)

**C19.** Green: Letter body (3–23) brackets faith: open exhortation (3–4) and closing call (20–23); between them “texts” + applications marked by “these/these are” (8, 10, 12–13, 16, 19).  
- Quote: “Between these poles Jude lays out a series of ‘texts’ that reference the OT, Jewish literature, and apostolic prophecy … Following each of these ‘texts,’ our author explains how the text applies … Jude includes a rhetorical marker … ‘these’ heretics … (vv. 8, 10, 12–13, 16, 19).”  
- Locus: L1399  
- Targets: `jude`, `gene-green`

**C20.** Green: Rhetorical strategy distances readers (“beloved”) from heretics (“these”) and draws them to Jude, wider community, revelation, and God; heretics destined for condemnation “marked from times of old.”  
- Quote: “Jude’s rhetorical strategy is to distance the readers from the false teachers who have integrated themselves into the church while at the same time drawing them to himself and the wider Christian community, to divine revelation, and to God himself.”  
- Locus: L1401  
- Targets: `jude`, `gene-green`

**C21.** Green: Body opens with disclosure of purpose: planned “common security” (3a) abandoned under pressure; outsiders promote altered grace → sexual vice and denial of Christ’s authority; paraenetic letter calling to action.  
- Quote: “Though the author has planned to address his readers about the great theme of their ‘common security’ (v. 3a), he is strongly pressed by circumstances to change tack. Outsiders have come among the congregation, promoting an altered doctrine of grace that promotes sexual vice and that, in the end, is a denial of the authority of Christ.”  
- Locus: L1420  
- Targets: `jude`, `gene-green`

**C22.** Green: Ἀγαπητοί is transitional body-opening address; familial bond; peaks in moral exhortation; family-letter context for instruction.  
- Quote: “Far from being stereotypical, the address retains its emphasis on the familial bond that exists between members of the Christian community. … Unsurprisingly, its use in letters peaks in contexts of moral exhortation.”  
- Locus: L1431  
- Targets: `jude`, `gene-green`

**C23.** Green: Against Reicke: περί + gen. and dual “to write” (present then aorist) signal a *previous* planned letter about “common security,” not the present letter; present content is “defense of the faith.”  
- Quote: “The use of the περί clause in verse 3a suggests a previous correspondence in contrast with the purpose that now compels Jude to write. … the content of Jude is not about the ‘common security’ itself but rather about the defense of the faith (v. 3b).”

- Targets: `jude`, `gene-green`

**C24.** Green: “Common security” (κοινῆς … σωτηρίας) adapts Greco-Roman “national security” / common safety language (Philo, Diodorus, Xenophon, Isocrates) to the church’s stance “against the hostile forces of the age.”  
- Quote: “Jude adopts the language of a principal social and political concern of the age and adapted the concept to the setting of the church. … He has purposed to write to the church about their ‘common security’ as the people of God who stand against the hostile forces of the age.”

**C25.** Green: ἀνάγκην ἔσχον — constrained by circumstances of heretics’ entrance (γάρ v. 4); purpose is παρακαλῶν to contend (ἐπαγωνίζεσθαι) for once-for-all handed-down faith; hortatory aim, not mere information.

### II.B.1 Text/comment 5–8

**C34.** Green: Strategy for 5–19: ancient “texts” (OT, Pseudepigrapha, apostolic prophecy) + commentary applying them to heretics; first unit Exodus/angels/Sodom; third Cain/Balaam/Korah; second Michael/devil; fourth Enoch; fifth apostolic testimony.  
- Quote: “Jude builds his denunciation of the heretics by drawing on ‘texts’ from the OT (vv. 5–7, 11), OT Pseudepigrapha (vv. 9, 14), and apostolic prophecy (vv. 17–18).”  
- Locus: L1495  
- Targets: `jude`, `1-enoch`, `michael-archangel`, `gene-green`

**C35.** Green: Three examples prefigure heretics by overstepping divinely established order despite privilege, then being judged; severity highlights gravity of transgression.  
- Quote: “Jude’s fundamental concern is to show how they transgressed or overstepped divinely established order. Also, Jude shows that whatever their privileged state was, they were subsequently judged for their sin.”  
- Locus: L1503  
- Targets: `jude`, `gene-green`

**C36.** Green: Selection of exodus generation / fallen angels / Sodom is not random; echoes Jewish interpretive strings (Sir. 16:7–10; 3 Macc. 2:4–7; CD 2.17–3.12; T. Naph. 3.4–5; m. Sanh. 10.3; cf. 2 Pet. 2:4–9) without dependence on one exposition.  
- Quote: “Although Jude is not dependent on any particular ancient exposition of these texts, he apparently knows and echoes this ancient interpretive tradition.”  
- Locus: L1505  
- Targets: `jude`, `1-enoch`, `gene-green`

**C37.** Green: “I want you to remember, although you know all this” — reminder formula of moral instruction; purpose not mere denunciation but exhortation (contend v. 3; keep love v. 21; rescue vv. 22–23).  
- Quote: “The use of the reminder formula at the head of the list of past judgments signals that Jude’s purpose is not simply to denounce but to exhort.”

- Targets: `jude`, `gene-green`

**C38.** Green: Prefers reading “Jesus” (Ἰησοῦς) as subject of exodus deliverance—best attested, most difficult, explains other variants (Metzger/Wikgren/Osburn); preexistent Christ typology (1 Cor. 10:4; John; Heb. 11:26; Bede).  
- Quote: “‘Jesus’ is ‘admittedly … the best attested reading among Greek and versional witnesses,’ according to Metzger along with Wikgren and Osburn. … This difficult reading best accounts for the rise of the other variants.”

**C39.** Green: ἅπαξ of exodus deliverance links to final gospel (v. 3) and undercuts heretics’ assumed immunity from judgment despite grace/salvation.
